chapter: Newark and first years in Harlem
title: Playing with Jelly Roll Morton: gangsters, bordellos and his sermons
summary: Butler describes Morton berating a singer, gangsters, rushing out the back door, and Morton's contradictory preaching about morals while running bordellos.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Remembering Jelly Roll Morton: the man, the band

blocks.x: I did it and so Jelly Roll and some man there was named Al somebody, wearing a big diamond ring, and Jelly Roll opened up, cursing the chick out, come up here you so and so: and sing a song, and don't you rush the tempo and you hear what I said, and she was crying. Get up there now and he started playing one of them gut bucket things--take that mute and put it in that half pocket and I did just that. I stayed there and Jelly Roll Morton and he was -- those poor women, was in awful shape and the gangsters come in, Jelly --he'd sing "Mr. Jellord," he was taking that stuff bad and come on round there -- was really getting straight.

So then it seemed like overnight, seeing that thing happen like it happen -- something happen and wouldn't nobody come to work. Can't go over there now, little later, little later, then we went to work and some guys come in there and Jelly Roll Morton say come on, let's get behind the piano and then make it out the back door and that's what we did and then

Jelly Roll Morton get out there and preach about the valuation of Negro man and the white man, dogs and roaches and things being equals and he would say, it was awful. A human / to dead police dogs in the backyard, so he would --

His name was Ferdinand Alexander Morton, so he was a stickler for morals and yet he was running all the bordellos. But that's the way he was. And so I just listened to him and I said, I ain't none of them kind of people, "Mr. Jelly Roll, and he said, "I wasn't talking to you. I'm talking about them people out there." (Unintelligible)
